extraction.name: CIFAR-10
extraction.description: A labeled subset of the tiny images dataset consisting of 60,000 32x32 color images across 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck) with 6000 images per class. The dataset is divided into 5000 training images and 1000 test images per class.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset by filtering out mislabeled images. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with search terms that are hyponyms of the main search term. Labelers were instructed to reject images which did not belong to their assigned class based on specific criteria.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data comes from the tiny images dataset collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU, which contains 80 million color images downscaled to 32x32 pixels spread across 79000 search terms. The images were collected by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collecting images for each search term, perfect duplicates and images with excessively large portions of white pixels were removed. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. For some experiments, data was whitened using the ZCA whitening transformation, and the 1000 least-significant directions of variance were deleted from the dataset. The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Labelers were given specific criteria for deciding whether to include an image in a class. The main test was whether the category name would be a likely answer when asked to give a single basic category to describe the main object in the image. Labelers were instructed to reject images with multiple prominent objects, line drawings or cartoons (unless photorealistic with internal texture), and to accept images with unusual viewpoints or partial occlusion. All labels submitted by labelers were personally verified.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal axes, likely caused by the way people take photographs - making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object. The search term used to find an image provides a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is divided into training and test sets for object classification experiments. Training set contains 5000 images per class, test set contains 1000 images per class. The dataset was used to test whether object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images.

name.evidence: We call this the CIFAR-10 dataset, after the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, which funded the project.

description.evidence: The labeled subset we collected consists of ten classes of objects with 6000 images in each class. The classes are airplane, automobile (but not truck or pickup truck), bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, and truck (but not pickup truck)... Finally, we divided the dataset into a training and test set, the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. The labeled subset we collected consists of ten classes of objects with 6000 images in each class... Since each image in the dataset already comes with a noisy label (the search term used to find the image), all we needed the labelers to do was to filter out the mislabeled images. To that end, each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all the images which were found with that class as the search term.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white, as they tended to be synthetic figures rather than natural images... We removed duplicate images from the dataset by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: In total, the dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32×32... To mitigate this, we decided to remove some of the least significant directions of variance from the dataset. We accomplished this by setting to zero those entries of the diagonal matrix D of equation (A.1) that correspond to the 1000 least significant principal components... Finally, we divided the dataset into a training and test set, the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: The labelers were instructed to reject images which did not belong to their assigned class. The criteria for deciding whether an image belongs to a class were as follows: The class name should be high on the list of likely answers to the question 'What is in this picture?' The image should be photo-realistic. Labelers were instructed to reject line drawings. The image should contain only one prominent instance of the object to which the class refers. The object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is still clear to the labeler... Furthermore, we personally verified every label submitted by the labelers.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: The images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal. For example, the colour of the top-left pixel is correlated to the colour of the top-right pixel and the bottom-left pixel. This kind of symmetry can be observed in all pixels in the faint anti-diagonals of the covariance matrix. It is probably caused by the way people take photographs – making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object... The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Finally, we divided the dataset into a training and test set, the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class...
